The Tsongas Center isn’t proving to be a home ice advantage to the UML hockey team these days. The River Hawks dropped to 1-5 on home ice and New Hampshire’s 3-0 Hockey East victory Friday night marked UML’s second straight home shutout defeat along the banks of the Merrimack River. “Tonight was not our best effort,” said head coach Norm Bazin. “I didn’t think we started poorly, as I thought the first period was a back-and-forth battle. From there, we took some untimely penalties in the second period, which seemed to drain a lot of our energy. We had to kill off a 5-on-3 and two other penalties. On the third, I think it was a missed assignment, followed by two net-front tip goals. We have to clean that up if we’re going to have success tomorrow.” Both teams were looking for their first Hockey East win of the season. New Hampshire (4-4-1, 1-2-1) received it thanks to goaltender Michael Stimpson, who posted a 21-save shutout and also picked up an assist on the third goal. Nick Ring led the Wildcats with a goal and assist effort. Austin Elliott made 27 saves for the River Hawks (2-7, 0-3 AE). Five players had two shots on goal for UML – defenseman Thomas Stewart, Kolton Sisson, defenseman Josh Mori, defenseman Dominic Payne and Tobias Pitka. After a scoreless first period, the game got away from the River Hawks in the second period. The Wildcats scored on their final two shots of the period against Elliott to take a commanding 3-0 lead after 40 minutes. Ring opened the scoring at the 1:56 mark. Elliott was standing tall in net for UML until late in the period when Nick VanTassell sent a shot past him at the 17:29 mark. Just 75 seconds later, with UNH on the power play, goalie Stimpson sent a pass to Ring, who found Ryan Johnson for a backbreaking goal. UNH outshot the hosts 26-15 over the first two periods. New Hampshire will host the rematch Saturday (7 p.m.) at the Whittemore Center. Junior Justin Godbout-Garon (Québec City, Canada) of UMass Lowell has been named to the America East All-Academic Team, as announced by the conference on Friday morning. In his first season at UMass Lowell, Godbout-Garon was quick to leave his mark, ranking first on the team with 11 points, including being tied with a team-high four goals while ranking second with three assists. The junior caught fire midseason, posting four straight games with two points, highlighted by a goal in three straight matches, also earning him America East Offensive Player of the Week honors. “I’m really proud of Justin for earning All-Academic Honors,” said head coach Kyle Zenoni. “He represents everything we want in a student-athlete at UMass Lowell. His commitment, work ethic, and leadership both on and off the field have been outstanding. title: Offensive Woes Continue for River Hawks in 3-0 Home Loss to UNH - NGSC Sports
content: On Friday night, the UMass Lowell River Hawks returned home to the Tsongas Center to host the University of New Hampshire Wildcats, looking to turn around a 1-4-0 record on home ice. Sitting at 2-6-0, it marks just the fourth time in their Division I history that the River Hawks have started a season with that mark. Under head coach Norm Bazin, UML entered the night 21-19-3 against UNH. Historically, the Wildcats have won 23 all-time series against Lowell and recorded 15 shutouts overall (including eight during Bazin’s tenure). The River Hawks entered the contest following a road split at Colgate. Starting in goal for UNH was Michael Simpson, a transfer from Providence who entered the night at 3-4-1 with a 2.57 goals-against average and an .892 save percentage. The River Hawks countered with Austin Elliott (1-4-0, 4.26 GAA, .874 save percentage). A scoreless first period saw both teams struggle to generate offense. Each squad failed to capitalize on a power play, extending UMass Lowell’s streak to 16 consecutive penalty kills and 28-of-32 overall. UNH held an 11-7 advantage in shots on goal after 20 minutes. The Wildcats broke the deadlock at 1:56 of the second period when Nick Ring redirected a point shot from Malte Vass past Elliott for his fourth goal of the season, assisted by Ryan Johnson. UMass Lowell’s penalty-killing unit held strong midway through the frame, erasing two more penalties—including a 5-on-3 power play—to make it 18 straight kills and 30-of-34 overall. However, UNH extended its lead at even strength when Nick Van Tassell scored his first goal of the season from the low slot, assisted by Ryan Philbrick and Vass. The Wildcats then made it 3-0 on a power-play goal by Johnson—his second of the year—from the left side of the net at 18:41, with assists going to Ring and goaltender Simpson. UNH outshot UML 15-8 in the second period, taking a 26-15 shot advantage and a 3-0 lead into the final intermission. The River Hawks, who fell to 0-5-0 when trailing after two periods, were unable to mount a comeback in a scoreless third period. — UMass Lowell Hockey (@RiverHawkHockey) November 7, 2026 UNH netminder Michael Simpson stopped all 20 shots he faced to earn his first shutout of the season. “It’s great to get our first Hockey East win,” UNH head coach Mike Souza said after the game, adding that he liked the way his team played with the lead and noting that the penalty kill came through when needed most. On the opposing bench, Bazin was candid about his team’s performance. “Not our best effort,” Bazin said, emphasizing that the River Hawks must generate more offense both at 5-on-5 and on the power play, while signaling that line changes are coming for Saturday night’s rematch. title: Professor Kristen Johnson Receives National Innovation in Education Award - University of New Hampshire
content: Kristen Johnson, associate professor of biotechnology at the University of New Hampshire at Manchester, has received the American Society for Cell Biology’s (ASCB) 2026 Innovation in Education Award for her innovative approaches to science education and commitment to expanding research and professional development opportunities for students. Johnson was selected by an ASCB committee for her impact spanning classroom instruction, undergraduate research, industry partnerships, and national initiatives designed to make scientific learning more accessible. For Johnson, innovation in education begins with a simple idea: Students learn best when they have opportunities to experiment, make mistakes, and discover answers for themselves. That philosophy has shaped her teaching style at UNH Manchester, where she has developed research-based courses that give students hands-on experience with scientific inquiry. Rather than following prescribed experiments with predictable results, students design their own investigations, develop hypotheses, analyze data, and present their findings. Johnson has developed four distinct course-based research experiences spanning molecular biology, protein biochemistry, and cell culture. These experiences have become an integral part of the life sciences curriculum, with most students now completing at least one research-based course during their degree programs. In one molecular biology course, students previously used synthetic biology to create programmable biosensors. Today, they use freshwater flatworms to investigate human diseases. In the cell culture course, they investigate how drugs affect fat cell development to better understand metabolic diseases. These projects expose students to the challenges and discoveries of scientific research while helping them build problem-solving, collaboration, and communication skills. Johnson’s impact extends beyond the classroom. Over the past nine years, she has mentored more than 90 student researchers in her laboratory, which investigates the molecular mechanisms of pancreatic cancer and other diseases. Her approach has helped students contribute to published research, present scientific findings, and pursue advanced degrees. Johnson has also worked to expand access to biotechnology career opportunities through NH CLIMBS (Collaborative Learning through Industry Internships and Academic Mentorship in Biotech for Students), a program she developed to connect students with industry-relevant research and technologies. The initiative provided paid, hands-on research opportunities that allowed students to collaborate with biotechnology companies without having to leave campus for traditional internships. Building on this commitment to accessible, industry-relevant training, Johnson also organized summer Cell Culture Crash Course workshops for New Hampshire students whose institutions lacked access to advanced laboratory coursework. Supported by funding from NH INBRE and EPSCoR, the workshops combined technical training with industry visits, professional networking, and financial support for participants. Together, these initiatives helped reduce geographic and financial barriers to valuable research and training experiences, preparing students for opportunities in the biotechnology industry. Beyond UNH Manchester, Johnson serves as a co-principal investigator of the National Science Foundation-funded Cell Biology Education Consortium, a national initiative that helps faculty and undergraduate students publish their scientific research. Through mentorship, editorial support, and professional development programs, the consortium has supported more than 10 publications over the past two years. These efforts reflect Johnson's commitment to making meaningful scientific experiences available to students from a wide range of backgrounds, while preparing them for careers and further study in the life sciences. Johnson will be recognized at ASCB's annual Cell Bio meeting in San Diego this December, where she will deliver a presentation titled Innovation in Education: Why Uncertainty Is the Starting Point, Not the Obstacle. Drawing on her own experiences as a first-generation college student, Johnson's presentation will explore how embracing uncertainty, taking risks, and learning through trial and error can lead to more effective teaching and meaningful educational change. "Rather than viewing imperfection as something to overcome, I argue that it is the foundation of creativity, resilience, and lasting growth," Johnson writes in her presentation abstract. It's a perspective that continues to guide her work at UNH Manchester: creating opportunities for students not simply to learn about science, but to experience the process of discovery firsthand. title: Questions linger over UNH polling after Scott’s Vermont election win - WCAX
content:
MONTPELIER, Vt. (WCAX) - Gov. Phil Scott’s victory over Amanda Janoo in Tuesday’s election is raising questions about pre-election polling that showed him losing the Vermont governor’s race. A September poll predicted Janoo winning by six points, 49% to Scott’s 43%. A second poll, released a day before Election Day, showed Janoo ahead eight points, 51% to 43%. But it was Scott who came out on top Tuesday, beating Janoo by seven points. Polls are only accurate if the pollsters survey a representative cross-section of likely voters. The Scott team and experts say the UNH Survey Center erred in who they included in their survey. “The political pundits were writing my obituary, and the UNH poll had us losing by about nine points. It looks like we’re going to win by over five, which is a 14-point swing,” Gov. Phil Scott said on election night. It’s the third election in a row UNH has underestimated Scott’s support. “The assumptions they made about who would turn out to vote were incorrect,” said Matt Dickinson, a Middlebury College political science professor. In recent years, polling outfits have struggled to get people to pick up the phone to achieve an accurate sample. Instead, UNH and other pollsters use a preselected panel of participants to fill out the poll. Dickinson says in assembling their panels, UNH overestimated younger voter turnout, who may skew toward Janoo, and underestimated the turnout of those over 65, who may skew toward Scott. “If you incorrectly make assumptions here as UNH did, that opt-in panel can lead you astray, and that’s what happened here,” Dickinson said. “We were very accurate in every other race, except the Vermont governor’s race,” said Andy Smith, one of the lead UNH Survey Center pollsters. He says they accurately predicted Vermont’s lieutenant governor, Congress, and constitutional amendments, in addition to other races across New England. He adds the Green Mountain panel is weighted to match the distribution of people in Vermont. “The thing I think they were misleadingly looking at is saying the weight of younger people is really the weight overall of all people, adults living in Vermont, not just voters.” Smith says voters need to be cautious when interpreting the results of any poll and that pollsters around the country are grappling with the right methodology to get an accurate representation of likely voters. He says it’s too soon to tell what they will do differently next election cycle and that they will take the next few weeks to do a post-mortem of their data. Experts also say polls can influence voter behavior, such as when and how people vote or donate money to candidates, believing one candidate is ahead or behind in the race. Dickinson says that may have played a role in the Scott-Janoo race. He suspects the national Republican Governors Association wouldn’t have poured a million dollars into Vermont on behalf of Scott if the poll was conducted differently. title: New Grant Will Support Research on Emerging Cold-Hardy Grapevine Disease - University of New Hampshire
content: Cold hardy grapes are the foundation of a thriving $400 million industry that includes wine production and agrotourism and stretches from the northern Midwest to the Great Lakes to the Northeast, including New Hampshire.  According to WineAmerica's 2025 Economic Impact Study, New Hampshire's wine industry supports an estimated 154,500 winery-related visits annually, generating approximately $29.5 million in tourism expenditures and contributing to local economies. However, cold hardy grapes are facing an emerging threat: a grapevine trunk disease caused by a species of fungi in the genus Fusarium. While Fusarium species are well known as pathogens of many crops, their role in cold hardy grapevine trunk disease remains poorly understood. Key questions include where disease-causing populations originate, how and when they invading the grapevines, or how to detect them early enough to inform management decisions. A new research project funded by the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture will investigate an emerging Fusarium-associated disease affecting cold-hardy grapevines. The project, “Exploring Fusarium Trunk Decline, an Emerging Threat to Cold-Hardy Grapevines in the U.S.,” is led by Xiaochen Yuan, assistant professor, and Suzanne Slack, adjunct research faculty, both in the department of agriculture, nutrition, and food systems. The project builds on several years of research by Yuan and Slack investigating the role of Fusarium species in grapevine decline in northern U.S. production regions. Previous vineyard surveys recovered Fusarium species from declining grapevines, and pathogenicity studies demonstrated that some of these isolates can cause disease in both cold-hardy hybrid and Vitis vinifera grape cultivars. Substantial yield losses have also been documented in vineyards affected by decline, highlighting the need to better understand the biology, distribution, and management of this emerging disease. The new project will expand this work across the Midwest, Great Lakes, and Northeast to determine the geographic distribution and genetic diversity of Fusarium populations associated with grapevine trunk disease, evaluate their ability to cause disease and mycotoxigenic potential, improve diagnostic approaches, and investigate factors that may influence disease development and management. “An important part is figuring out how widespread this problem actually is,” says Slack. “We have data from the Midwest, but since we've been here [in New Hampshire], we've already been in contact with local vineyards having this problem, and we did find Fusarium inside their samples.” The goal is to provide grape growers with practical tools for earlier disease recognition and science-based management recommendations that can reduce disease losses and protect vineyard productivity. “Right now, it takes almost two months to determine if it's the correct Fusarium. There are some species that are non-pathogenic that could be in the wood,” says Slack. “So we need to test if it's the one that's pathogenic or the strains that are just kind of hanging out. We want to develop a quick way to tell a grower, ‘Yes, it's here,’ so they can make quick management decisions.” “We won't say we'll completely eliminate it, but at least we can help our growers to manage it,” adds Yuan. The project also represents an important collaboration among UNH researchers, USDA-ARS scientist Kristi Gdanetz MacCready, Extension specialists, diagnostic laboratories, and grape growers across the region. Results will be shared with growers and industry professionals through Extension programming, publications, diagnostic resources, and regional outreach. title: What a UNH professor taught me about politics, disagreement and hate: Splaine - Seacoastonline.com
content: While a sophomore at the University of New Hampshire in 1967, I signed up for American History 101, taught by Professor David Long. Many UNH students remember him as a popular teacher with a booming, pleasant voice that made his lectures both fascinating and enjoyable. His classes incorporated his textbook, titled "The American Story" (McGraw-Hill, 1955) with tidbits of yarns he would tell us, almost like a casual chat. Instead of just dates and names, he put context into his lectures that encouraged an understanding of the year-to-year, decade-to-decade evolution of American history, along with the "why" of our history − good and bad − the tragic, as well as the human progress. His course led me to major in history, leading to my formal certification to teach high school history upon graduation.  Incidentally, my brother John also had his class.  He was one of our favorites. I remember that Professor Long's lessons taught that as our American experience evolves, the daily issues that challenge us need not divide us as human beings. Too often we hate one another just because we have differences of opinion. Opinion need not cause hate. I thought of Dr. Long during the past few weeks as I felt an inner tension about the pending Nov. 3 election. I know friends felt the same nervousness. Much was at stake, regardless of your party affiliation. Uncertainty is always tense. I watched many television news and news talk shows these past few weeks. I intentionally ignored social media and instead focused on a diversity of news, seeking to hear about varied ideas people had, their points of view, their fears about election security, and their concerns about voter intimidation. I tried to absorb the rhetoric of the candidates. I noticed that all candidates made things up at times, some more than others, and just about all candidates exaggerated the wrongdoings of their opponents. Such is electioneering − it happens everywhere, and likely goes back to the days of old Rome and Greece. The 2026 midterms are over, and two years − just 104 weeks − will pass, and those who don't support last Tuesday's results will soon have another day. During that time, wouldn't it be good for all of us to accept Professor Long's view of the American story and appreciate that we can each differ with one another. That's okay. That's politics. Everyone has an opinion. Yes, there are important issues about which we differ. But even the life and death issues will change over time and hating one another doesn't improve our efforts to find answers.  We can be passionate about our positions on issues without hating one another to the point of violence, or of not even trying to talk with one another. We need leaders who will work together to resolve our commonality, work toward our common good, reject greed and the "me-first" or "me-only" philosophy, and find ways of friendship and peace. If all that sounds like a lecture, credit it to a wonderful late UNH professor named David Long. Our Republican and Democratic leaders, with their varying philosophies, will be going to our State House in coming weeks, or traveling to assume their duties in Washington. Let them be passionate, and fight for their causes. But let's hope they put their energies into positive accomplishments for us.  And let's hope they can do that job together. Observation:  I'm impressed that Texas U.S. Senator-elect James Talarico speaks of love, and isn't ashamed of it. Today's quote. "Regardless of individual beliefs, which we all respect of each other, it is amazing to think about all of the voting locations across the state and the country where folks just like you volunteer to ensure fair elections are executed with accuracy, efficiency, transparency, and friendliness."  - Brian Gibb, Ward 1 Moderator in a note to his poll volunteers who worked into the night on Tuesday.  Let's thank them for protecting our democracy. Variously since 1969, Jim Splaine has been New Hampshire state senator for six years and state representative for 24 years.  He was six-term Portsmouth Assistant Mayor for 12 years, nine-term city councilor for 18 years, elected as Police Commissioner, and served on the School Board.  jimsplaineportsmouthNH@gmail.com

BOSTON (WHDH) - Andy Smith, Director of the UNH Survey Center, said his polling showed that the midterms were a referendum on President Trump. Smith said motivated democrats showed up at the polls and helped drive the results. “It was a question if those people who are least likely to vote, younger voters, they are the ones who are driving the energy, in the democratic party, it appears they turned out and voted,” Smith said. This was evident in the Senate race in New Hampshire, where democrat Chris Pappas beat republican John Sununu. “Among Sununu supporters, about 60 percent had nothing to do with Trump, but among Pappas supporters, 87% said their vote was a vote against Donald Trump,” Smith said. Smith said that motivation carried down the ballot. Voters often choose candidates from the same party once they enter the voting booth. “They typically vote straight ticket; the party that gets them to the polls in the first place, they are going to vote for that party all the way down the line,” Smith said. Smith said republicans will now have to decide what comes next. “They have to decide if [it is] Trump’s party or a more ideologically conservative republican,” Smith said. title: Voices of UNH Manchester Wildcats Series: Meet Mechanical Engineering Technology Major, Kieran McCurdy, '25 - University of New Hampshire
content: Are you considering a future in mechanical engineering technology? Meet Kieran McCurdy, class of '25 at UNH Manchester, whose journey offers a firsthand look at the value of this dynamic program. Whether you’re a prospective student or simply curious about what makes UNH Manchester stand out, Kieran’s experience highlights the unique opportunities, hands-on learning, and career advantages waiting for you. For Kieran, the decision to attend UNH Manchester was driven by the program’s practical focus and its strong industry connections. He shares, “UNH Manchester is a hub for all these different companies. When you graduate, there are all these job opportunities that you can go into.” The campus’s location in the heart of Manchester, NH, puts students close to leading engineering firms and tech companies, opening doors to internships, networking, and career placement right after graduation. Kieran’s experience in the mechanical engineering technology program is marked by a diverse curriculum and hands-on learning. He explains, “My favorite thing about the mechanical engineering technology program at UNH Manchester is the array of classes you take. I get to learn about thermodynamics, electrical, and mechanical stresses all in one degree.” This means students gain expertise across multiple engineering disciplines, preparing them for a wide range of careers. Classes at UNH Manchester teach students not only theory; they also show them how to apply their knowledge in real-world situations. Kieran notes, “I’m taking a 3D printing class. With this class, I’ve been able to level up my 3D printing skills because I’m able to think more critically about the way I design.” The program’s modern facilities, including advanced labs and equipment, further support this hands-on approach. Highlights from Kieran’s Mechanical Engineering Technology Journey One of the highlights of Kieran’s journey was the capstone project, where he worked alongside fellow students to build robots. He explains, “You work on a team with three to four engineers, and you’re building robots. You’re required to make three 3D printed parts per robot and three machine parts per robot.” The project culminates in a friendly competition that lets students test their creations and celebrate their achievements. This experience encourages teamwork, critical thinking, and practical problem-solving. Kieran’s time at UNH Manchester has been filled with opportunities to apply his skills in real-world settings. As an automation intern at Freudenberg, Kerian gained valuable exposure: "We had an inspection machine there. I worked on the wire diagram for that machine," he shares. These internships, made possible by the campus’s industry connections, help students build their resumes and prepare for the workforce. Beyond the curriculum, Kieran appreciates the small class sizes and the collaborative environment. Faculty are invested in student success, and peers share a passion for innovation and problem-solving. The campus’s supportive community and access to advanced technology make it an ideal place to grow as an engineer. Graduates of the mechanical engineering technology program at UNH Manchester often go into the following fields: As graduation approaches, Kieran is confident in his path. “After I graduate, I plan on working as a process engineer. I want to work at either BAE or DEKA because these are companies that are at the forefront and are located right next to UNH Manchester.” He credits the program for giving him the practical skills needed to succeed: “I got those practical skills that I need to work as a process engineer.” Watch and listen to Kieran's full story about his mechanical engineering technology journey at UNH Manchester and his career goals: Choosing UNH Manchester means choosing a campus that’s deeply connected to industry, offers hands-on learning, and supports your professional ambitions. title: The Democracy Summit: UNH’s Democracy Infosession - The New Hampshire
content: On Wednesday Oct. 7, the Responsible Governance and Sustainable Citizenship Project (RGSCP) hosted The University of New Hampshire’s (UNH) Democracy Summit. This is RGSCP’s first event for the fall semester, in which they will be answering questions like “What does democracy mean?” and, “Is the concept of democratic governance in jeopardy?” The wide range of faculty in attendance offered many topics for students, as well as the community, to hear about throughout the entirety of Wednesday. The Democracy Summit organized by the RGSCP held many seminars to educate the public about civics. The summit saw college students, high school students, other faculty, and many more. The overall outcome of the summit was considered a success and works to pave the way for more events throughout the school year. Alynna Lyon, professor of Political Violence and International Affairs at UNH, spoke on “Can Democracy Create Peace?” In her section, Lyon covered what constitutes a democracy, as well as how it creates peace between countries. A pair of democracies do not make war. The more democratic two countries are, the less their chance of mutual violence. Lyon touched on the Kantian Triangle, a framework for causes of peace linking democracy, economic interdependence, and membership in international organizations. The triangle was created by Immanuel Kant in his essay “Perceptual Peace” which proposed elements and conditions for lasting peace throughout many countries. With high levels in the Kantian Triangle elements, the incidence of fatal disputes drops by 95%. “We are seeing declining levels of democracy throughout the globe,” said Lyon. Components of democracy include regular elections for the most powerful government positions, near universal franchise meaning the right to vote, secret balloting, civil liberties and political rights, such as free press and free speech, and competitive political parties; not everybody wins all the time. Lyon’s talk included many statistics and research about democracy, violence, as well as the differing tactics that have been taken to promote democracy in other countries. Through this research, Lyon argued that democracy is good for human beings. Aspects correlated with democracy such as literacy rate, education levels, income levels, and life expectancy all increase in democratic states. “Democracies are going down, violence at the international level is going up,” said Professor Lyon. Another section focused on The New Hampshire Declaration of Independence with Sue Siggelakis, a professor of Political Science and Justice Studies at theUNH. Siggelakis spoke about how John Adams and his associates worked together to create pressure on the people in the Continental Congress to cause action. From there, the declaration encouraged independence. Siggelakis helped break down the language and how the writers emulated a lot of the British style of diction. Siggelakis also emphasized the organization, and how this gives insight into what the writers were feeling about the current conflicts within the states. The New Hampshire Declaration of Independence states themselves free and independent, and exemplifies the British syntax such as “whereas” within the text, as well as following along with the other colonies. “And Whereas We of this Colony of New Hampshire have the Example of several of the most Respectable of our Sister Colonies before us for Entering upon that most Important Step of a Disunion from Great Britain, and Declaring ourselves FREE and INDEPENDENT of the Crown thereof…” Another chunk of the Declaration says, “WE DO, therefore Declare that it is the opinion of this Assembly that our Delegates at the Continental Congress should be instructed, and they are hereby Instructed to join with the other Colonies in Declaring THE THIRTEEN UNITED COLONIES, A FREE AND INDEPENDENT STATE…” Here we see the call to action that  Siggelakis referred to that the colonies were pushing the Congress towards. Another section of the Democracy Summit was led by James Wible, a professor of economics at UNH. “Ten Remarkable Economic Features of the U.S. Constitution” focused on parts of the U.S. Constitution that set up our country for its current economic standpoint. Professor Wible included honorable mentions such as: importation of slaves could be banned after 1808, no compensation was given to slave owners upon freeing of the slaves, the eighteenth amendment instating the Prohibition then repealed by the twenty-first amendment. The Democracy Summit by the RGSCP was a step in presenting civics education to those within the community.
